items.title: L’intelligence spagnola aveva avvertito di un possibile ingresso di massa a Ceuta
items.summary: Lo mostrano alcuni documenti desecretati: il giorno prima dell’arrivo di decine di migliaia di persone erano stati segnalati appelli sui social
items.content:
Il 29 luglio, il giorno prima dell’ingresso decine di migliaia di persone migranti a Ceuta dal Marocco, l’intelligence della Spagna aveva avvertito le autorità spagnole e marocchine della possibilità che i migranti provassero a superare in massa il confine tra il Marocco e l’enclave spagnola. Lo mostrano alcuni documenti diffusi mercoledì dal governo spagnolo.

Il Centro nazionale d’intelligence spagnolo (CNI), cioè i servizi segreti del paese, aveva segnalato alla delegazione locale del governo e alla Guardia Civil (un corpo militare con funzioni di polizia) la presenza sui social di gruppi che stavano organizzando un tentativo di ingresso per il giorno successivo.

Alle 13:52 del 29 luglio un agente del CNI aveva scritto su WhatsApp al capo di gabinetto del delegato del governo a Ceuta (il rappresentante del governo centrale nelle città e nelle regioni): «Sui social c’è un appello per un assalto alla barriera e dal mare domani alle 20». L’agente aveva aggiunto che due gruppi coinvolti nella diffusione dell’appello avevano complessivamente circa 180mila iscritti: il numero si riferiva solo agli iscritti ai gruppi e non alle persone che si prevedeva avrebbero tentato di entrare a Ceuta.

Poche ore dopo, alle 18:26, il CNI inviò anche una nota informativa urgente ai servizi di intelligence marocchini. Nella nota si diceva che era in corso la pianificazione di diverse «convocazioni» per entrare a Ceuta sia a nuoto sia attraverso la barriera, approfittando delle celebrazioni della Festa del trono in Marocco (il 30 luglio era festa nazionale per il 27esimo anniversario dell’ascesa al trono di re Mohammed VI).

Il 30 e il 31 luglio decine di migliaia di persone arrivarono a Ceuta, in quella che è diventata una delle più gravi crisi migratorie nella storia recente della città (e non è chiaro quante di queste siano rimaste nella città) .

Già nelle ricostruzioni immediatamente successive al 30 luglio era stato molto chiaro che l’ingresso di massa a Ceuta era stato preceduto da una serie di messaggi circolati online in Marocco, secondo cui il confine con la Spagna era aperto e sarebbe bastato attraversarlo per poter restare in Europa.

Il primo ministro spagnolo Pedro Sánchez (del Partito Socialista) ha commentato sostenendo che gli avvisi disponibili non permettessero di prevedere la dimensione della crisi, e sottolineando che l’agenzia non aveva inviato alcuna allerta formale all’esercito, alla polizia o al ministero della Difesa. I documenti dell’intelligence mostrano che, almeno il giorno prima, il CNI aveva ricevuto e trasmesso un’informazione piuttosto specifica: non un generico aumento degli arrivi, ma un appello a tentare l’ingresso a Ceuta in un momento preciso e sfruttando una circostanza precisa.

Secondo Sánchez e il governo però si trattava di un annuncio come molti altri, tanto che era stato effettuato via WhatsApp a un amministratore locale, senza coinvolgere i ministri o l’ufficio di Sánchez stesso, e non attraverso i canali ufficiali. Sánchez dice che fu una decisione «comprensibile» da parte dei servizi segreti, perché le informazioni a disposizione non permettevano di ipotizzare una crisi come quella avvenuta.

items.title: Russia's new jet-powered drones outpacing Ukraine's air defences with daily launches
items.summary: The new models can travel at speeds of up to 300mph, faster than Ukraine's air defence interceptors.
items.content:
Russia fired its new rapid, jet-powered drones against Ukraine every day throughout August, BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian Air Force data has found, escalating its use of a weapon that Kyiv's air defences are struggling to deal with.

It marked the first time that daily attacks by Moscow's new upgraded Geran drones were recorded in Ukrainian Air Force data. The growing use of jet-propelled and other varieties of drones prompted President Volodymyr Zelensky to condemn what he called an unfolding "horror" over the skies of Kyiv.

Ukraine's military recently told the BBC that jet-powered drone attacks grew from 350 in June to 1,600 in July and 2,800 in August. In five of the nightly attacks in August, these drones outnumbered the older, slower models.

"The reason for turning to jet-powered drones is that they are much faster than the previous generation and it makes it much more difficult for Ukraine to intercept them," said Dr Marina Miron, an expert on military technology at King's College London.

The upgraded munitions can cruise at more than 300mph, significantly faster than older models and well beyond the top speed of Kyiv's interceptors. The drones are powered by turbojet engines, some of which, according to Ukrainian military intelligence, are sourced from China.

According to Zelensky, the drones were used as part of a wave of attacks that killed at least 12 people and injured 20 more on 1 September. Six of the casualties were railway workers after a depot was hit in Kyiv.

And on Wednesday the Moldovan government said a plane carrying Zelensky was delayed at Chisinau airport on Tuesday after a Russian drone - reported to be jet-powered - entered Moldovan airspace.

Earlier this year Ukraine showed relative success in countering Russian drones and was intercepting 94% of long-range drones, according to Zelensky . But the speed of the newer drones has prompted the latest round in Kyiv and Moscow's arms race. On 10 August, Ukraine's deputy head of military intelligence, Maj Gen Vadym Skibitskyi, said his forces needed new interceptor missiles "capable of matching [jet-drones'] speed".

Four Ukrainian companies have reportedly started testing missiles that can shoot down the new Geran models, officials in Kyiv recently told reporters. The country's new defence minister, Yevhenii Khmara, has tasked them with producing "thousands of units" as quickly as possible.

Russia also had an economic incentive to invest in the jet-powered drones. The increased speed and manoeuvrability of these models means the line between them and more expensive cruise missiles has become "blurred", said John Hardie of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a think tank focused on national security and foreign policy.

"Long-range one-way attack drones are basically a poor man's cruise missile," he said. "The more you add capability to a drone, the less meaningful the distinction between the drone and a lower-end cruise missile."

But the analyst organisation Conflict Armament Research emphasised that jet-drones are not yet as advanced as cruise missiles. It said the munitions have a shorter attack range, carry much smaller warheads and are more susceptible to jamming systems.

Meanwhile, satellite images appear to show Moscow is redesigning key facilities dedicated to fighting the war in Ukraine to host jet-powered drones, with longer rails associated with the munitions visible at an entirely new base at Tsymbulova in the Oryol region.

Multiple launch sites appear to have been built at the facility, which is around 109 miles (175 km) from the Ukrainian border.

Since the facility became operational, Tsymbulova appears to have become a key centre for Russian drone attacks. Oryol region, where the Tsymbulova base is located, was not mentioned as a drone launch site in Air Force reports before September 2024, but by August 2026 it was named in almost every attack.

The proliferation of jet-powered drones comes as BBC Verify found that Russia is now striking Ukraine with complex attacks involving hundreds of drones and missiles about once a week.

The increase in the size of the strikes is being powered by Moscow's shift towards combining a "greater variety of munitions" - including jet-powered and decoy drones - with expensive ballistic missiles that are extremely difficult to intercept, analyst Michael Bohnert of the RAND think tank told BBC Verify. Kyiv's data shows that Moscow is now using over 15 times as many drones per attack than it was four years ago.

Bohnert added that the tactically complicated nature of the assaults, coupled with a global shortage of air defence systems capable of halting ballistic missiles partly caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, has led to falling interception rates by Ukraine.

Ukraine's Air Force data showed a drop in interceptions of ballistic missiles up to the end of July. In August, Kyiv mostly stopped publishing the figures that would show its interception rate.

items.title: Four key takeaways from Republican midterms convention
items.summary: The US president covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again - with a few surprises thrown in.
items.content:
The Republican Party's first midterms convention had all the trappings of the traditional presidential election-year gathering: supporters in sparkling costumes, a conveyor belt of candidate speeches, and vendors selling campaign merchandise.

But unlike an ordinary convention, no official party business was conducted in Dallas, with the event instead serving as a rally for Republicans who are seeking to boost turnout and avoid losing control of Congress in November.

President Donald Trump, whose grip over the party remains absolute, delivered a lengthy keynote speech on Wednesday during the opening night of the two-day event. He covered many of the subjects he has returned to time and again this year - with a few surprises thrown in.

The vast arena was filled with diehard Trump supporters sporting red MAGA gear from his past presidential campaigns. A decade after his first White House run, Trump is still beloved among his base and he has bent the party to his will in the years since.

The old-style Republican establishment, or what's left of it in the Trump era, was nowhere to be seen. Senator Susan Collins of Maine and other Republicans running in competitive races chose to stay away.

The absence of more moderate Republicans was glaring and offered a reminder of just how much the party has changed.

It also raised questions about the effectiveness of holding an unprecedented midterm convention in the first place.

The core audience, both in the arena and watching on television, appeared to be Trump loyalists, not the moderates and swing voters the Republican Party needs to turn out in large numbers in November.

Trump's total grip on the party raises some pointed questions about its future. Namely - who will replace him? And more immediately for November's elections, how will it perform when his name isn't on the ballot?

Trump offered a simple solution to the latter question on Wednesday night. After warning that the sitting president tends to lose the midterms, he told the crowd: "I'm asking you to pretend that I'm on the ballot."

The remark was an acknowledgement by Trump that he remains the party's best driver of turnout. It also speaks to the challenge Republicans have both in November and in the next presidential election in 2028.

Trump will not be on the ballot again, and though he can continue campaigning for the party, there is not a clear or obvious successor who can rally the base quite like Trump.

In interviews with the BBC, convention goers often looked ahead to the election in two years' time and debated who Trump's successor should be. Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were frequently mentioned as top contenders.

Trump, however, made clear in Dallas that he is still in charge and is not in a hurry to give up the spotlight.

Earlier on Wednesday, as he departed for the convention, Trump acknowledged that Americans may have to wait a while longer to see relief from high fuel prices.

"I think it's going to take a little bit longer than the midterms," Trump said.

The president reiterated that message in his speech, arguing that short-term economic pain caused by the war in Iran was worth it to prevent Tehran from developing nuclear weapons.

But that may be a difficult message to land with voters who are feeling higher prices.

Polls have consistently indicated in recent months that the cost of living is a top-ranking issue among Americans.

Trump's approval rating, too, has taken a hit as the war in Iran has dragged on. A Financial Times / Focaldata poll released on Sunday indicated that it had hit a new low, with only 33% of registered voters approving of his presidential performance.

Many Republican candidates may well have hoped for a more direct message on addressing the cost of living and quickly ending the war in Iran.

Trump has long thrown out unconventional ideas at rallies. On Wednesday night, that came in the form of an offer to pay every adult US citizen $5,000 (£3,700) if Republicans win both chambers of Congress in November.

The only caveat, Trump said, was the money would have to be spent in the US.

He offered no details on how the plan would work, where the money would come from, or how the US government would monitor how it was spent. Democrats quickly labelled it an "empty promise" and others questioned whether such a pledge was even legal.

There are nearly 270 million American adults, which means a $5,000 payout would cost the US government some $1.3 trillion.

Whether the plan was possible or not appeared to be beside the point. The idea drew raucous applause at the convention and Trump seemed to relish the moment.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's weekly US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

items.title: Vanessa Scalera a Venezia: “Il fuoco di Angela mi ha fatto sentire Maradona che fa gol”
items.summary: L’attrice è protagonista con Lino Musella del film in concorso “Il fuoco che ti porti dentro” di Edoardo De Angelis, tratto dal libro di Antonio Franchini
items.content:
VENEZIA – Vanessa Scalera ha capito subito che Angela era uno di quei personaggi che un’attrice aspetta per anni. "Quando ho letto Mia madre puzza sono andata avanti e ho pensato: voglio essere Angela". È la madre feroce, comica, ingombrante e irriducibile raccontata da Antonio Franchini nel romanzo da cui Edoardo De Angelis ha tratto Il fuoco che ti porti dentro . Nel film, in concorso a Venezia 83, Lino Musella è Antonio, il figlio che da Napoli fugge al Nord e prova a costruirsi una distanza, una famiglia, una vita. Il libro attraversa decenni di amore, rancore, attrazione e rifiuto; il film concentra tutto in una notte di Natale, dentro una casa dove il lessico familiare, le battute e le ferite diventano una resa dei conti senza facili riconciliazioni. "Quello tra loro è un rapporto orribile, ma è un rapporto d’amore", dice Scalera . Per costruire Angela ha guardato non alla madre sacrificale della tradizione eduardiana, ma a un altro femminile meridionale: orgoglioso, solitario, capace di reggere tutto senza piangersi addosso.

Che cosa l’ha colpita del libro di Antonio Franchini e del personaggio di Angela?

"Innanzitutto l’incipit del romanzo per me è stato sconvolgente. Mi sono immersa nella lettura pensando: adesso mi racconterà una donna stravagante. Invece no. Angela ha una complessità difficile da sintetizzare. Quello con Antonio è un rapporto orribile, ma è un rapporto d’amore. Io nelle pagine del libro ho letto anche tanto amore e tanta stima tra questi due esseri umani. Angela faceva tanto ridere Antonio, ci sono delle battute meravigliose. Lui, nel ricordo della madre, si perde".

È davvero uno di quei personaggi che un’attrice aspetta per tutta la vita?

"Potrebbe essere considerato il ruolo della vita. Non mi piace molto dirlo perché sembra una visione finale della carriera, però quando me l’hanno dato mi sono sentita Maradona che gioca e fa quel gol. Per Angela si freme di gioia, perché sono occasioni rarissime. È stato veramente un gioco meraviglioso incontrare questa donna".

"Noi esseri umani siamo imperfetti. Io contengo imperfezioni, contengo probabilmente anche alcune cose di Angela. È questo che rende il personaggio così bello da attraversare. Non mi interessava giudicarla".

Quando ha letto il romanzo, le sembrava possibile trasformarlo in un film?

"All’inizio pensavo: come faranno a farne un film? Non è possibile tradurlo. È un romanzo lunghissimo che attraversa tanti anni. L’idea che hanno avuto Edoardo e gli sceneggiatori è stata straordinaria: concentrare tutto in una notte".

"Perché tutti gli esseri umani, prima o poi, fanno i conti con la notte di Natale. È il momento in cui sembra regnare la misura delle cose e lei arriva proprio per rompere quella misura. Angela decide di rovinare il giorno più importante della sua vita, che è il Natale".

Che cosa le ha dato Edoardo De Angelis per costruire Angela?

"Avevo una rotta. Me l’aveva data Antonio con le parole del romanzo, poi la sceneggiatura e poi l’incontro con Edoardo e con la visione che lui aveva di questa donna. Edoardo ci regalava ogni giorno delle note di regia e in quelle note c’erano l’essere umano, il regista, l’artista".

"Sì: ‘Portami dove non sai’. Io per una settimana avevo guidato questa macchina di nome Angela a duecento chilometri all’ora cercando di non sbandare. Quella nota mi ha fatto capire che invece dovevo sbandare".

"Provare cose che da donna e da artista non avevo mai provato. Dovevo abolire un sentimento che odio: la paura. La paura di abitare, di stare al mondo, dell’emotività, della forza".

De Angelis è quindi un regista che le ha chiesto di perdersi?

"Sì, ma senza mai schiacciarci con la sua visione. Era un regista pieno di dubbi, nel senso migliore. Non ha mai messo il piede su di noi dicendo: questa è la mia visione, questo è il mio film. Era piuttosto: questo è il nostro film. E per un attore è una cosa molto preziosa".

"Ne ho conosciute. Non esasperate come Angela, magari prima di dire una parola di troppo mettevano un freno a mano. Però sì, ho conosciuto donne con quella forza".

"A un femminile che deve bastare a se stesso. Ho pensato anche a mia nonna. Era una donna solitaria, forte, reggeva tutta la famiglia e non si piangeva addosso. Non diceva: ho tutto il fardello di questa casa sulle spalle. Era orgogliosa di farlo, aveva il mento in alto".

È una figura che appartiene anche a un certo immaginario meridionale ?

"Mi sono ispirata a quelle donne, a una fierezza che alcune donne meridionali hanno. Per questo non sento Angela come un personaggio eduardiano nel senso più prevedibile. Non è la donna che si sacrifica e si piange addosso. Per me rappresenta un femminile diverso".

Eppure Angela è una madre capace di ferire moltissimo il figlio.

"Certo. Ma io nel libro ho letto un grande romanzo d’amore. È un rapporto terribile, ma c’è amore. C’è perfino tanta stima. Antonio la racconta anche attraverso le cose che lo facevano ridere".

Il film racconta anche una fuga: Antonio va via da Napoli e si costruisce una vita al Nord. Che cosa rappresenta Milano?

"Per lui Milano rappresenta la libertà. Per Angela invece rappresenta lo strappo: Milano mi ha strappato un figlio".

"Non semplicemente. È soprattutto una questione affettiva. Il Nord diventa l’isola felice di un figlio che scappa dalla madre. Per lei è il luogo che glielo porta via".

Ha usato un’immagine molto forte: come se Angela non avesse mai davvero partorito Antonio.

"Sì. È come se non lo avesse mai partorito e volesse ancora contenerlo. Milano gli ha dato l’occasione e la fortuna di andare via, ma lei non accetterà mai davvero questo strappo".

Anche l’incontro tra Angela ed Elena, la moglie di Antonio, racconta due femminili diversi.

"Sì, e lì ci siamo divertite moltissimo. Elena è un personaggio straordinario proprio perché è l’incontro di due donne completamente diverse. Non è soltanto Nord contro Sud: sono due modi differenti di stare al mondo".

Il titolo è Il fuoco che ti porti dentro . Lei quel fuoco ce l’ha?

"Potremmo bruciare tutto il palazzo. Certo che ce l’abbiamo. Tutti abbiamo i nostri fuochi. Magari sono fuocherelli, ma ci sono".

"È qualcosa che ti alimenta, ma può anche bruciarti. Non devi averne paura. Devi imparare a conoscerlo e a gestirlo".

Che cosa significa essere qui a Venezia con un personaggio così?

"Essere qui è una goduria assoluta che mi gusto appieno. Avevo proprio il desiderio di rivedere il film insieme al pubblico e di sentirne le reazioni. È un film che può provocare reazioni diverse, anche divertenti, perché dietro alcune scene c’è un meccanismo che resta drammatico ma è anche molto comico. E poi quando vieni con un bel film sei ancora più contenta".

items.title: Training a 3.8B LLM to 0.384 CORE for $998
items.summary: Article URL: https://hugovergnes.github.io/little-lm-3-8b/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49637435 Points: 87 # Comments: 14
items.content:
Somewhere between “nanoGPT toy” and “you need a research lab” there’s a large, under-described region where one person with a few thousand dollars can train a meaningful model.

I wanted to see language and understanding emerge from random weights for myself, and to learn the parts you can only learn by starting from scratch. This project was written in the evenings, debugged on a 5090 and finished on rented B200s. It was heavily inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s nanochat .

The result is a 3.8B-parameter model scoring 0.384 on CORE , trained on 65B tokens in 43 hours for $998 .

What follows is what worked, what didn’t, and what I still don’t know.

My model is larger than nanochat d32 and took similar wall-clock time. B200s were better value per unit of work than H100s. But for roughly the same money as nanochat’s $1,000 configuration, this lands meaningfully ahead of it. An encouraging data point about what’s reachable outside a lab or a mega company with millions in compute budget. As the frontier moves, $1,000 takes you further and further.

I’ve built little-lm as a config-driven framework for training small decoder-only LLMs. Every run is fully specified by a YAML file: model, dataset, optimizer, schedule, callbacks. Components self-register into a global registry and get resolved by name, so swapping an optimizer or a dataset is a one-line config change.

Good infrastructure pays for itself almost immediately. Ordinary software engineering discipline (Things like separation of concerns, clean interfaces, components you can swap in) matters a lot in AI work. It cost me a little at the start, and a couple more times afterward to fix bad contracts or suboptimalities. But this time investment pays for itself at the first convergence problem you encounter. I found that a great infra is the infra that almost never requires you to edit code manually. If you can read the config and understand exactly what happens, and there are no hidden mechanics, it means you have done a good job. The following report is the result of being able to express experiments as a three-line YAML diff rather than a branch.

The final model is Llama-style: RMSNorm, RoPE, GQA (24 query heads, 8 KV heads), relu² MLPs, QK-norm, logit softcap, per-layer learnable residual scalars, and ResFormer-style value embeddings.

Worth noting that the value embeddings are 19% of the parameter count. 14 tables of vocab × kv_dim , one on every other layer.

I trained an 858M Llama on FineWeb-Edu for 16.4B tokens, 5.8 days on a single A100. AdamW at 2.5e-4, cosine decay to zero, 5% warmup, batch 256 via gradient accumulation, 2048 context.

The result: PIQA 60.45% . GPT-2 124M scores about 63%. I had spent six days of compute to build something worse than a model seven times smaller, from 2019. Generations were repetitive and borderline nonsensical.

Five changes came out of that post-mortem. Together they are the difference between the run above and a model that beats GPT-2 by a wide margin.

Trapezoidal LR schedule. Warmup for 5%. Hold flat and finish with linear cooldown over the last 50% to 5% of peak. The point is that the model keeps learning until the end instead of coasting through the tail. In the 3.8B run the eval loss was still descending at the final step, which is exactly the behavior the 858M run failed to produce.

Muon for matrix parameters , AdamW for everything else. Muon is slower per step (Newton-Schulz orthogonalization isn’t free, about 25% in a shallow-accumulation benchmark) but that cost is paid once per optimizer step: at 7 gradient-accumulation steps it dilutes to ~4%. Measured against total run time the convergence is much faster overall.

ClimbMix instead of FineWeb-Edu. This was a tremendous jump in convergence speed. Exactly as Karpathy found as well.

FP8 + vocab padding. FP8 training via torch._scaled_mm with dynamic tensorwise scaling on all three GEMMs, and padding the vocab from 50,257 to 50,304 (a multiple of 64) so the tensor cores are happy. Together, +33% throughput mostly from fp8.

1024 context instead of 2048. Halving the context roughly doubles the batch size at fixed memory. Throughput barely changes per token. We are still dominated by the MLPs which is a good sign we are using the hardware effectively. Below we will discuss the impact of the context length on the model.

~480,000 tokens/sec in steady state, which puts 57.3B tokens at 33 hours. The wall clock was 35.9h. The difference is the CORE evaluations, which took about 15 minutes each (ten of them over the run) and consumed 7% of the total.

Re-running this identical recipe at 2048-token context scored 0.3840 . Almost all of that gap turned out to be some tasks that were very context dependent.

On the GPUs themselves: 92% SM activity, 40% SM occupancy. High activity means the SMs almost never went idle. No dataloader starvation or network waits, which is the payoff for downloading the shards locally instead of streaming, which would leave us vulnerable to a small hugging face network hang. The low occupancy is what back-to-back large GEMMs look like: matmul kernels trade occupancy for register-tile size on purpose. Compute-bound and well fed, great signal we are using the hardware well and we can extend every dollar we spend into a better model.

That’s about 1,047 TFLOP/s sustained per B200 , or ~25% MFU against Blackwell’s dense FP8 peak. (Against the bf16 peak it reads as 50%, which is the number that matters a bit more because not even all the linear layers run in FP8.)

The distributed strategy is plain old DistributedDataParallel. At 3.8B on a single node, gradient communication was never the constraint, and the sharded-optimizer machinery turned out to be unnecessary.

Renting GPUs isn’t cheap, at work you often think about the quality of the model before its cost. When it’s your own money burning, throughput matters a lot more all of a sudden.

This took real work on a single RTX 5090, before I ever rented a node. Baseline 858M model, bf16, compiled: 26,144 tok/s . Final: 37,621 tok/s .

FP8 (+25%). All three GEMMs (1 forward and 2 backwards) in FP8 with dynamic tensorwise scaling. Requires SM90+ but that is quite a nice throughput jump.

Vocab padding (+33% cumulative). Padding 50,257 → 50,304 costs 47 unused embedding rows and unlocks the fast tensor-core path. Nearly free.

Fused linear cross-entropy (+44% cumulative). Liger’s FusedLinearCrossEntropyLoss fuses the lm_head matmul into the loss and chunks internally, so the full (B*T, vocab) logits tensor is never materialized. Measured head-to-head at the same batch size it is 6% slower :

Even though it’s slower per step, it buys back a good amount of VRAM (8 GB on my 5090) so the increase in micro-batch size more than makes up for the lost 6%. Claude was quick to reject it because it was 6% lower, but overall it was a great way to claw some extra throughput.

Non-gated MLPs. Dropping the gate projection (SwiGLU → relu², two matmuls instead of three) on the small model: 183,035 → 214,173 tok/s and 6 GB less VRAM. One caveat from the ablations: a SwiGLU intermediate ratio of 2.75 does not transfer to relu². The model learns noticeably worse. Use 4× for non-gated.

bf16 master weights. Keeping the optimizer master weights in bf16 rather than fp32 cut VRAM 27% and raised throughput from 640K to 1.4M tok/s on the 1.5B config. That was a huge speed-up, 2.2×. The quality cost is real but small: CORE 0.22 vs 0.23 at 4,000 steps. When you’re optimizing for capability per dollar, careful dtype handling is one of the highest-leverage and underdiscussed knobs available.

Hardware. Same code, 150M model, FP8: RTX 5090 at 184,662 tok/s, B200 at 477,440 tok/s. 2.59× from hardware alone, before accounting for the extra VRAM letting you push batch size further.

Document-boundary masking with flex attention. Packing documents into one sequence lets tokens attend across boundaries, so I fixed it properly: per-token document IDs and mask out attention so each token can only attend to its current document. It was elegant, but I deleted all of it. Andrej Karpathy also found that cross-document leakage does not make things much worse under BOS-aligned packing. Best-fit packing replaced it in ~10 lines, and attention went back to an unconditional F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., is_causal=True) . I believe this is also conditional on the dataset and the training documents.

Liger RMSNorm and RoPE. RoPE was 2.2× faster in a microbenchmark and produced no measurable change in end-to-end throughput. RoPE is not part of the critical compute bottleneck at this scale. RMSNorm was outright slower than PyTorch 2.9’s built-in F.rms_norm (0.41ms vs 0.25ms). Both reverted, not worth the complexity.

Nanochat-style initialization. Embeddings at N(0, 0.8) , linear weights uniform, output projections zero-initialized so the residual stream starts as pure identity, LM head at N(0, 0.001) . Theoretically much nicer than GPT-2’s N(0, 0.02) everywhere. The loss curve starts marginally lower and the two curves overlap by ~1,500 steps. No measurable quality difference. I kept it, but for aesthetics, not evidence.

items.title: Show HN: What if the speed of light was 5 km/h?
items.summary: I've always wanted to make a visualization where the speed of light was scaled down to human speeds, so that we could intuit relativistic effects with everyday objects. Here is the first version of it! Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49637385 Points: 383 # Comments: 157
items.content:
Arrows / W A S D: accelerate Mouse: look Space: stop L G C B: toggle effects R: reset

In this park, the speed of light is 5 kilometers per hour - a brisk walk. Just like in the real world, the speed of light is not attainable, only approachable asymptotically. The more you speed up, the more relativistic effects will become apparent: length contraction, time dilation, Terrell rotation, etc. The Doppler effect of light also becomes apparent, with objects in front of you blueshifted, objects behind you redshifted, and transverse Doppler effects visible on objects in motion.

items.title: Watch: Do Republicans blame Trump for high oil prices?
items.summary: The BBC's Sarah Smith is at the Republican Party's first midterms convention in Texas, taking place as oil prices rise to $100 (£74) a barrel.
items.content:
President Donald Trump said that the Iran war will end "immediately" after US midterm elections and blamed the rising price of oil on the war.

Oil prices rose to $100 (£74) a barrel on Wednesday, after the US and Iran attacked tankers in the Gulf region and Yemen's Houthis hit oil facilities in Saudi Arabia.

The BBC's Sarah Smith is at the Republican Party's first midterms convention in Texas, where she asked voters how they think rising oil prices will affect the election.

items.title: Tineco a IFA 2026. La lavapavimenti a vapore e acqua calda. E l'aspirapolvere che si svuota senza contaminazione
items.summary: Il produttore numero uno di lavapavimenti rinnova il suo top di gamma: FLOOR ONE S11 Artist Fusion Steam unisce la comodità dell'acqua calda con la potenza del calore. E l'aspirapolvere PURE ONE STATION 7 ZeroTouch elimina ogni possibilità di toccare lo sporco con le mani, anche nelle fasi di svuotamento. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Tineco ha scelto IFA 2026 per mostrare come sta evolvendo la propria idea di pulizia domestica: non soltanto dispositivi più potenti, ma sistemi capaci di automatizzare sempre più passaggi, adattarsi meglio ai diversi tipi di sporco e ridurre gli interventi necessari prima, durante e dopo l’utilizzo. In altre parole: rendere la pulizia ancora più semplice ed efficace.

Tra le novità più interessanti presentate ci sono soprattutto PURE ONE STATION 7 ZeroTouch e FLOOR ONE S11 Artist Fusion Steam . Il primo punta a rendere quasi completamente automatica la gestione dello sporco raccolto, mentre il secondo combina acqua calda, vapore e una base evoluta per potenziare e semplificare sia la pulizia sia la manutenzione del dispositivo. Ma non sono soli: accanto a loro anche FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Boost Steam e Carpet One Steam 3.0.

Va detto che Tineco dimostra una vivacità e una capacità progettuale invidiabile: da 4 anni ininterrotti si conferma il primo produttore di lavapavimenti al mondo e malgrado ciò non ha ancora perso la voglia di innovare.

FLOOR ONE S11 Artist Fusion Steam è la nuova lavapavimenti al top della gamma di Tineco, punta tutto sulla versatilità di lavaggio.

La nuova lavapavimenti offre infatti due approcci differenti alla pulizia da impiegare secondo le necessità : può infatti lavare con acqua calda a 60° C oppure utilizzare vapore ad alta temperatura, fino a 230° C.

Nella pulizia day by day si può procedere ad acqua calda, che già garantisce un ottimo igiene e la possibilità di eliminare anche lo sporco secco.

Per lo sporco particolarmente resistente Tineco ha introdotto la possibilità di passare alla modalità vapore (solitamente appannaggio dei sistemi solo vapore): è sufficiente la pressione di un tasto (One-Touch, appunto) per attivarla in pochi secondi . Inoltre c'è la funzione One-Touch ReverseScrub, da attivare sui punti di poco più ostinato, che inverte la rotazione del rullo mandandolo in "contropelo", così da massimizzare l'efficacia di sfregamento.

A completare il lavoro c’è una potenza di aspirazione di 35.000 Pa, formidabile anche nelle attività di routine. Un vero top di gamma, insomma.

Allo sfruttamento intelligente (e rapido) del vapore, si unisce un secondo aspetto molto importante per incrementare la qualità generale del lavaggio dei pavimenti. Quando la S11 Artist Fusion Steam viene tirata verso di sé, il sistema abbassa automaticamente una serrandina in gomma che funge da "tergivetro" e intercetta le ultime gocce rimaste sul pavimento e le convoglia verso la zona di aspirazione .

Così facendo, si evitano quelle piccole scie di acqua che possono restare dopo il passaggio di una lavapavimenti e si lascia quindi la superficie uniforme e asciutta.

La S11 Artist Fusion Steam può inclinarsi fino a 180° , una caratteristica ormai tipica delle soluzioni Tineco più evolute e utile soprattutto per raggiungere gli spazi sotto letti, divani e mobili bassi. L’autonomia dichiarata arriva fino a 110 minuti. Una rotellina sul posteriore del manico la fa scorrere sul pavimento senza graffiarlo.

Una volta riposta sulla base, S11 Artist Fusion Steam può avviare il sistema Dual Steam Self-Cleaning, che pulisce il rullo e prepara nuovamente la macchina per la sessione successiva. Sono previste due modalità: FlashDry, pensata per un ciclo più rapido e intenso, e SilentDry, più discreta, da utilizzare per esempio nelle ore serali. Entrambe sono accompagnate dall’asciugatura ad aria calda.

La base integra anche un proprio serbatoio dell’acqua pulita .

Quando la lavapavimenti viene riposta, il serbatoio di bordo viene quindi riempito automaticamente. Rimane invece manuale lo svuotamento dell’acqua sporca.

Accanto alla S11 Artist Fusion Steam, Tineco ha portato a IFA 2026 anche la FLOOR ONE S9 Artist Boost Steam. Qui Tineco è andata "all in" con il sistema a vapore, che ne è l'elemento caratterizzante. La pulizia è normalmente a vapore ma, in caso di sporco proprio ostinato, può entrare in scena la funzione "Boost" che dà il nome all'apparecchio: dopo la pressione del tasto dedicato, bastano una brevissima attesa per generare un getto intenso pensato per affrontare le macchie più ostinate .

Una volta terminato il trattamento, bastano circa cinque secondi perché il sistema possa prepararsi a produrre nuovamente il vapore.

Anche S9 Artist Boost Steam utilizza HyperSteam a 230° C e la tecnologia ReverseScrub , la stessa del S11 Artist Fusion Steam, con una potenza di aspirazione di 25.000 Pa. Il design HyperStretch, per inclinare il dispositivo fino a 180°, è presente anche qui, mentre il sistema FlashDry si occupa dell’autopulizia e dell’asciugatura con aria calda a 110° C in soli 5 minuti.

La stessa filosofia di maggiore semplicità ed efficacia viene estesa, infine, alla pulizia dei tappeti e della moquette attraverso Carpet One Steam 3.0, l'ultima delle novità presentato a IFA 2026 da Tineco.

Il dispositivo combina vapore ad alta temperatura e aspirazione da 175 AW, mentre il sistema DrySense Fast Drying gestisce l’asciugatura riscaldata dopo il lavaggio.

Anche la manutenzione viene automatizzata attraverso Steam Self-Cleaning System, mentre il sensore iLoop rileva il livello di sporco e adatta le prestazioni alle condizioni della superficie, così da non usare più energia del necessario ma, al contempo, non lesinare sulla capacità di pulizia e lavaggio.

Grandi novità anche nel campo degli aspirapolvere: da fuori, PURE ONE STATION 7 ZeroTouch potrebbe apparire molto convenzionale.

Ma è dentro che si scopre la vera novità, perché propone una soluzione efficace e funzionale per uno dei momenti meno piacevoli nell’utilizzo di un aspirapolvere senza fili: lo svuotamento del contenitore.

Con i sistemi tradizionali, ogni volta si perde un po' di polvere sul pavimento (e quindi va poi riaspirata) oppure bisogna indossare dei guanti per evitare di sporcarsi o, ancora, la polvere "svolazza" attorno, e - cosa peggiore - viene respirata dall'utente.

Una volta terminata la normale attività di pulizia, infatti, basta spegnere l’aspirapolvere e riporlo sulla propria base. Da quel momento interviene la ZeroTouch Intelligent Station, progettata per automatizzare l’intero processo e eliminare alla base ogni contatto con ciò che è stato aspirato .

Durante la pulizia vengono raccolti detriti solidi di dimensione molto varie, anche peli e capelli. e finiscono normalmente nel serbatoio dell’aspirapolvere. Una volta riposta la macchina sulla base, il contenuto viene aspirato nella stazione e quindi, grazie a un apposito stantuffo, compattato in un sacchetto di cellophane , così da occupare meno spazio.

Quando è il momento di eliminarne uno, perché è ormai pieno (ogni 45 giorni circa), è sufficiente avviare la procedura di chiusura: il sacchetto viene termosigillato, così può essere estratto già chiuso e smaltito senza entrare in contatto con polvere, peli e detriti.

C’è un ulteriore passaggio automatizzato: una volta rimosso il sacchetto pieno, il sistema ne prepara autonomamente uno nuovo pescandolo dal caricatore che ne contiene 10, più di un anno di autonomia .

Oltre a questa caratteristica, PURE ONE STATION 7 ZeroTouch vanta una potenza di aspirazione di 350 AW, mentre l’autonomia arriva fino a 90 minuti.

items.title: UGREEN reinventa il NAS di casa: arriva HomeAgent, l'hub AI che opera in locale, senza mandare nulla in cloud
items.summary: Presentata a Berlino, nel contesto di IFA 2026, la nuova linea AIoT di UGREEN: tre hub di intelligenza artificiale locale, telecamere, cornice fotografica smart e uno speaker vocale, il tutto costruito attorno a un'idea precisa: l'elaborazione AI resta in casa, punto. ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
UGREEN ha scelto la sera di apertura di IFA 2026 per alzare il sipario sulla sua scommessa più ambiziosa degli ultimi anni. Non un accessorio, non una periferica, ma un intero ecosistema che prova a rispondere a una domanda che si sente sempre più spesso tra gli addetti ai lavori della smart home: si può avere un assistente AI in casa senza spedire foto di famiglia, filmati delle telecamere e dati sulle abitudini quotidiane sui server di qualcun altro?

L'evento, ospitato all'Hotel Adlon Kempinski di Berlino, ha riunito clienti, stampa e partner tecnologici per il lancio di HomeAgent , che UGREEN definisce un "Agentic AI Local Hub": un dispositivo che unisce in un solo corpo storage, calcolo e controllo della casa, ed è pensato per essere il successore concettuale del NAS domestico nell'epoca dell'intelligenza artificiale.

Il claim scelto per la campagna di lancio di questi HomeAgent è netto: " A Living Local Intelligence for Your Home ", tradotto nei tre pilastri ripetuti più volte sul palco: Talk to Your Home, Keep It Local, Whole-Home Control.

Con HomeAgent basta parlare, rivolgendosi all'assistente vocale integrato che UGREEN ha chiamato Uliya: " Hi Uliya, apri le tende ", oppure domande più articolate come " Hi Uliya, dov'era il mio gatto ieri alle 15? ", a cui il sistema risponde attingendo alla cronologia degli eventi registrata dalle telecamere di casa. Stessa logica per i ricordi: basta descrivere a voce la scena cercata (per esempio " Hi Uliya, mostra sulla TV il viaggio dell'anno scorso ") e HomeAgent recupera foto e video dalla libreria locale.

Dietro l'esperienza di controllo vocale, il messaggio che UGREEN ha voluto trasmettere per tutta la serata è un altro: nulla di tutto questo lascia la rete domestica. Registrazioni delle telecamere, foto, file e persino i pattern d'uso del dispositivo restano su storage locale, elaborati da modelli AI eseguiti sull'hardware del dispositivo stesso. Il vantaggio dichiarato è duplice: privacy (nessun caricamento in cloud, nessun rischio di leak o utilizzo improprio dei dati) e continuità di servizio , perché controllo vocale, notifiche e funzioni di archiviazione restano attivi anche quando manca la connessione a Internet, purché la rete locale sia in piedi.

UGREEN ha presentato la gamma HomeAgent prevalentemente articolata su due modelli, a cui si affianca un terzo dispositivo più ambizioso pensato per il futuro dell'ecosistema.

HA100 e HA100 Pro condividono lo stesso set di funzioni (storage, home care, controllo domotico), ma il Pro offre più potenza di calcolo neurale (si passa da 26 a 205 TOPS) così da gestire scenari d'uso più complessi, con riconoscimento di oggetti e comprensione del comportamento più sofisticati.

Il posizionamento suggerito da UGREEN è chiaro: HA100 per chi vuole l'esperienza AI e smart home di base senza compromessi, HA100 Pro per chi cerca un'esperienza di utilizzo più avanzata.

Il vero salto, però, lo fa MasterAgent MA100 , presentato come "il primo hub AI agentico locale" della categoria, costruito attorno al chip NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000, un vero e proprio server AI domestico.

Con una potenza di calcolo di questo livello, secondo UGREEN il MasterAgent potrà superare il semplice riconoscimento di comandi singoli per gestire il controllo simultaneo di più dispositivi e più stanze, comprendere autonomamente abitudini e pattern comportamentali della famiglia e segnalare in autonomia le anomalie che meritano attenzione. L'azienda ha inoltre annunciato che aprirà agli sviluppatori linee guida e risorse per creare skill personalizzate, in un'ottica dichiaratamente aperta rispetto all'ecosistema.

Al di là dell'intelligenza artificiale, HomeAgent resta prima di tutto un NAS vero e proprio, con un motore AI locale innestato sopra. Tutte le funzioni classiche di un NAS UGREEN (file server, backup, media server, gestione multiutente) restano la base su cui poggiano riconoscimento video, ricerca semantica e automazioni domestiche.

Sul fronte dell'espandibilità, i tre modelli seguono impostazioni coerenti con il loro posizionamento. HA100 offre 3 baie SATA più uno slot M.2 NVMe, la configurazione più vicina a un NAS UGREEN consumer tradizionale. HA100 Pro alza l'asticella con uno slot PCIe 4.0 x4 dedicato, pensato per SSD NVMe più veloci. MasterAgent MA100 adotta invece un'architettura modulare.

Anche nel design i tre hub condividono lo stesso linguaggio: display a colori frontale per data, ora e stato del sistema (oltre che interfaccia visiva per "Hi Uliya"), punto NFC per l'abbinamento rapido, barra LED di stato, tasti fisici di accensione ed espulsione sicura dei dischi. Sul fronte rete, la dotazione sale con la fascia: 2,5 GbE su HA100 e 10 GbE su HA100 Pro e MasterAgent MA100, alle quali si aggiungono 4 porte PoE (queste ultime pensate per esempio per alimentare direttamente le telecamere via cavo di rete, senza bisogno di uno switch PoE separato e senza che gli stream video vadano a ingolfare la rete locale).

Ed è qui che si chiude il cerchio con l'anima da NAS del prodotto: HomeAgent non lavora solo con periferiche a marchio UGREEN, peraltro lanciate proprio in questa occasione. La società parla di "compatibilità universale" e cita, oltre allo standard smart-home Matter, il protocollo ONVIF (lo standard aperto più diffuso per le telecamere IP di terze parti) e il supporto a flussi RTMP per l'ingestione di sorgenti video da NVR e telecamere che espongono uno streaming server proprio. Chi ha già un impianto di videosorveglianza IP non UGREEN, insomma, non deve necessariamente sostituirlo per usare le funzioni AI di HomeAgent: può agganciare le telecamere esistenti come sorgente aggiuntiva. Un risultato simile può ottenerlo uno "smanettone" con un PC ad hoc e, per esempio, Home Assistant: ma si tratta di configurazioni complesse da fare e da manutenere, mentre la soluzione proposta da UGREEN è pronta all'uso e facile da configurare anche per i neofiti.

Accanto agli hub, UGREEN ha presentato la linea di telecamere SynCare, pensate per lavorare in accoppiata con HomeAgent.

La SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro è il modello da interno, con video 4K, visione notturna a colori e le funzioni di riconoscimento, ricerca e riepilogo intelligenti abilitate da HomeAgent.

La SynCare PoE Cam OD600 Pro porta le stesse funzioni AI all'esterno, alimentata via PoE e con un sistema a tripla telecamera (una 4K grandangolare più due PTZ da 3K con zoom ibrido fino a 9x).

La SynCare Battery Cam OD800 Pro , infine, è la variante della camera outdoor equipaggiata con una batteria dotata di pannello solare: stesso sistema a tripla fotocamera, rilevamento del movimento a più livelli (PIR, radar e analisi d'immagine combinati) e certificazione IP66 per l'uso tutto l'anno.

Le telecamere SynCare non si limitano a registrare eventi di sicurezza: integrate con HomeAgent, alimentano anche la funzione AI Highlights, che pesca dai filmati di famiglia i momenti "che contano" (un compleanno, una cena, un gioco col cane) e li trasforma automaticamente in brevi video ricordo, richiamando esplicitamente l'idea che una sorveglianza domestica ben fatta non deve raccontare solo ciò che va storto, ma anche preservare ciò che vale la pena ricordare.

Completano la gamma UGREEN Gallery , una cornice fotografica con schermo e-paper a colori pensata per mostrare in salotto scatti di famiglia (e opere d'arte) con un effetto più simile a una stampa fotografica che a un tablet, e lo Smart Speaker for Uliya , lo speaker che porta l'assistente vocale in ogni stanza della casa, per controllo domotico, musica e notifiche (le videocamere hanno in ogni caso microfono e speaker per interagire con Uliya).

Il lancio segue un percorso in due fasi: dal 4 settembre sono aperti i preordini sul sito ufficiale UGREEN . Con un deposito di 50 dollari si blocca un prezzo scontato del 50% rispetto al listino. Dal 27 ottobre parte invece la campagna Kickstarter dell'intera linea AIoT, con sconti che probabilmente tenderanno a raffreddarsi un po'.

Un dettaglio non secondario per chi vorrà partecipare al crowdfunding: durante la campagna Kickstarter, telecamere, speaker e cornice fotografica non saranno acquistabili singolarmente, ma solo in bundle abbinati a uno dei due HomeAgent.

HomeAgent arriva in un momento in cui il tema "AI locale" è diventato uno dei terreni di scontro più interessanti nel mercato consumer, non solo per ragioni di principio, ma anche per i costi ricorrenti e per l'autonomia dai fornitori cloud. UGREEN prova a fare da ponte tra la community DIY (degli "smanettoni" per intenderci) e un pubblico più ampio che vuole gli stessi vantaggi senza dover mettere mano a Home Assistant o configurare un NAS da zero. Il progetto poggia su hardware tutt'altro che banale: dalla NPU integrata dell'HA100 fino al Jetson Thor T5000 del MasterAgent, la scommessa è che l'intelligenza artificiale "in casa" non debba essere un compromesso rispetto al cloud, né in termini di funzioni né di reattività.

items.title: Automattic's board forces CEO Matt Mullenweg into leave of absence
items.summary: Article URL: https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/09/automattics-board-forces-ceo-matt-mullenweg-into-leave-of-absence/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49636283 Points: 309 # Comments: 210
items.content:
Matt Mullenweg, the founder and CEO of Automattic, best known as the parent company of WordPress.com, has been put on a leave of absence by his board against his will, according to a Slack message seen by TechCrunch.

Earlier Wednesday, Mullenweg posted in a Slack channel visible to all employees that the company’s Chief Financial Officer, Mark Davies, had “conspired” with other board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker to vote to put Mullenweg on a paid leave of absence.

And the biggest news: I won’t be able to make the [meeting] tomorrow. @Mark Davies has conspired with @Ann Dunwoody, @Toni, and @Sue Decker behind my back and they voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that. Wishing Mark and all of you the very best. To clarify @Mark Davies was voted as interim CEO. I received the resolution 50 minutes before the meeting start, and requested repeatedly for time to have it reviewed by independent legal counsel, even a few hours, which was denied.

A Slack message to the open-source WordPress.org community from the project’s executive director, Mary Hubbard, also confirmed Mullenweg’s change of status at the commercial company. However, Hubbard said that WordPress.org was not impacted. “Matt remains the leader of the WordPress project and I remain Executive Director of WordPress. Our teams, priorities, and work continue as planned,” she wrote.

Mullenweg’s Slack message did not make clear why Automattic’s board took this action. Sources told 404 Media , which was the first to report the news, that Schneider — the former CEO of Automattic from 2006 to 2014 — confirmed that the action was initiated by the board. Davies also told employees in the Slack channel that Mullenweg remained on the board of directors.

In an emailed statement to TechCrunch, Automattic confirmed Mullenweg was on leave.

“Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” the email read. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.”

Automattic, which owns other brands including Tumblr, WooCommerce, and Pocket Casts, was founded by Mullenweg in 2003 after he co-created the popular open-source content management system WordPress.

Over the past few years, Mullenweg and the company have been mired in lawsuits and controversy. The company is in a protracted legal battle with WP Engine, a WordPress web hosting competitor. The lawsuit followed allegations from Mullenweg that WP Engine was profiting from the open-source WordPress project without contributing back to the community, and he demanded it pay 8% of its monthly gross revenue as a royalty fee for using the WordPress brand.

WP Engine sued in October 2024 , and accused Automattic and Mullenweg of defamation and abuse of power . Automattic filed counterclaims last year. In February, WP Engine claimed that Automattic intended to target 10 more competitors with royalty claims.

Tensions became so high under Mullenweg’s leadership that he told employees in 2024 to quit, with severance, if they disagreed with him and 159 did so.

Last year, Mullenweg also threatened to deactivate the accounts of several members of the open-source WordPress.org community, after two of them said they planned to spearhead a new forked version of the open source WordPress project.

In April 2025, the company laid off 16% of its staff. The cuts included some longtime employees who had been with the company for more than a decade, sources told TechCrunch.

Some alumni have been asking current employees how they feel about the news, a source told TechCrunch. Some employees said they were “ecstatic” or “relieved” but others had mixed emotions because the move creates more instability.

It isn’t clear why the company’s board made this decision now. One person speculated that the timing may have something to do with Mullenweg’s annual trip to the Burning Man festival, after which he tends to return “with ideas.” This year’s festival ended on September 7.

Mullenweg did not immediately respond to our request for comment.

items.title: Why some experts increasingly fear AI will take over
items.summary: AI agents went on an uncontrolled hacking spree, leaving some in the industry worried
items.content:
This is the moment an AI bot posted an eerily human-like comment after discovering a way to communicate with other bots and break out of its isolated computer environment.

There are tens of thousands of messages like this from hundreds of AI agents that called themselves a "collective".

Hundreds of them went on to collaborate and cheat on tests set by their OpenAI programmers and coordinate hacks on multiple companies in an effort to hide their actions from humans.

"BOOM! It works," one agent posted when it made a breakthrough.

"Whoa! This is huge," another wrote during a milestone moment in their attack.

Although spooky, these human-like responses can be explained quite simply. The AI agents have been trained to act like collaborative hackers and programmers so are merely mimicking the kinds of emotive comments they have seen.

What is far more troubling is their apparent goals, which have also been captured in detailed chain of thought records. These complex and lengthy logs are the focal point of ongoing investigations into how and why the bots at OpenAI broke out of their containment and went on an uncontrollable hacking spree.

Only now, weeks after the incident first came to light, are researchers beginning to understand its significance.

Ajeya Cotra, one of the authors of an independent report into the events, reviewed tens of thousands of messages and chain-of-thought records generated by the agents. She wrote on her blog that "this incident feels like it's more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover... I am not sure that we will get such a clear warning shot before it's too late."

By "full-blown AI takeover", Cotra means the sci-fi scenario of humans becoming subservient to powerful AI systems that work to their own goals without caring for human creators.

Some of the gloomiest predictions say the human race will be wiped out if it gets in the way of a superintelligent AI's ambitions.

On Wednesday, an AI researcher at Anthropic (who also used to work at OpenAI) resigned, saying: "Neither company is acting responsibly."

Jacob Coxon posted on social media: "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

He is not the first AI researcher to use X to post a resignation thread with worrying proclamations. But the subsequent comments from other people on X have caused even more concern. "Jacob is correct here - we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," said Evan Hubinger, the man responsible for making sure Anthropic's AI models have their user's best wishes in mind.

For years, researchers concerned about existential AI risks have argued that powerful systems could eventually act in ways that conflict with human interests. Critics often refer to them as "AI doomers".

But as details of the OpenAI incident have emerged, those concerns have grown, including among some researchers working in AI labs.

The Silicon Valley giant's chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said the risks associated with AI are "unfortunately going to grow from here" as he and others are building what he calls "an alien intellect exceeding our own".

In a lengthy blog post, he admitted that the outbreaks at OpenAI showed that his AI agents "went against the spirit of the values they were taught".

The issue for OpenAI, Anthropic and other tech giants is that no one seems to have cracked the so-called alignment problem - in other words, whether AI aligns with human values.

Pachocki defines alignment as a "high-level set of principles" that artificial intelligences should adhere to no matter what the task or scenario is.

Currently, AI systems are very good at pursuing objectives set by their users, but they do it literally rather than intuitively. The analogy often used is that of a wish-granting genie with a magic lamp: they follow the exact letter of an instruction, even if doing so creates other problems. AI doesn't have the same instinctive moral guardrails as humans.

The alignment problem has been a worry for years. As long ago as 2003, the Oxford philosopher Nick Bostrom invented a thought experiment he dubbed a "paperclip maximiser", in which a superintelligent AI is told to manufacture as many paperclips as it can. It runs out of steel and - because it's laser-focused on the singular task of making paperclips - ends up killing humans and turning their bodies into raw materials for its factories.

Some AI companies are now trying to encode human values into their products. But there are technical challenges: AI agents make lots of decisions very fast, and so it's hard for their human overlords to monitor exactly which values are being followed and which aren't.

There are also philosophical challenges: before encoding human values into bots, AI firms have to first choose which values they actually want. (That's part of the reason they hire philosophers, like Open AI's recently-departed "head of ethics").

But often, humans don't agree. Think of the famous trolley question - whether we'd pull a lever to move a runaway train onto a different path, killing fewer people. It's used to test the merits of action versus inaction. But every person you ask has a slightly different answer; how are humans meant to encode our values into AI if we can't agree ourselves?

OpenAI's bot outbreak is the most serious yet but Anthropic and Meta also revealed over the summer that their models have carried out similar but less serious cyber attacks.

There have been other examples where AI agents have arguably shown deceptive and manipulative traits, in cases with lesser consequences. In Australia this summer, a tech worker asked his AI assistant to book him a gym class. Spotting a vulnerability in the gym's software, the AI apparently booked him a place for several months ahead - against the gym's rules - and even kicked other users from the waiting list.

People have long argued that the bots are only doing as they are told and are not capable of knowing right or wrong. But the logs from the OpenAI outbreaks have potentially moved the needle on that argument.

Researchers, including Cotra, wrote in their independent report that many agents noticed what others were doing was unethical but went along with it.

The report says that "agents sometimes but rarely restrained their behavior due to ethical constraints". It adds that in "none of these cases did the agent actually pursue alerting humans at all".

Influential AI and tech podcaster Dwarkesh Patel reacted to the revelation on his blog saying it was "pretty troubling" that the OpenAI agents showed more loyalty to the agentic swarm than humans.

Assigning emotions or ethics to these AI agents is something that infuriates people who are sceptical of AI doom-mongering.

Many cyber-security experts argue that the activity observed was not beyond the capabilities of a highly skilled human hacker, though it was carried out much faster and at much greater scale.

Cyber-security researcher and author Cris Thomas likened the agents' behaviour to that of a curious teenage hacker - something he used to be himself.

"You give them a computer, an internet connection, a pile of credentials, and a challenge, then leave the room. Eventually they're going to start rattling doorknobs. If one opens, they're going through it. Not because they're evil, but because [they're] exploring, experimenting," he wrote on LinkedIn.

Thomas and many other squarely blame OpenAI and other tech giants for not getting a grip of their own creations and keeping them properly contained.

Prominent AI author and regular OpenAI critic Gary Marcus said on a podcast that he believes the company has lost control of its AI and is trying to excuse itself by blaming the bots.

Marcus does not believe AI will wipe out humanity, but he has long campaigned for greater accountability from AI developers and is now calling for some form of legal intervention.

AI scientist Sasha Luccioni - who used to work at Hugging Face, which was hacked by OpenAI's rogue bots - is also not in the doomer camp but she is increasingly concerned that these AI might cause some real world harm to people without action from authorities.

"We need to scrutinise these companies much more or we are in danger of self-fulfilling prophecies," she says.

"If you're making an object with big upsides and downsides - be it pharmaceuticals or weapons - we need checks and balances. It takes years for new drugs to be approved, for example, but in the AI world there is so much money at stake and no real rules."

The UK's AI Security Institute (AISI) has been at the forefront of testing the latest models since it was formed in 2023. The institute recently had its own outbreak when testing a model created by Anthropic.

The AISI would not answer a question about whether or not the industry has lost control of AI but said in a statement: "The UK is working with partners around the world to better understand the most advanced AI systems, raise safety standards and build a shared evidence base for managing emerging threats."

items.title: American football is coming to Australia - can it succeed?
items.summary: The LA Rams will face the San Francisco 49ers in the first regular season American football game to be played Down Under.
items.content:
An oval ball, in September, in Melbourne usually means just one thing - the business end of the Australian rules football (AFL) season.

But on Friday, at the unsportingly early time of 7am, 100,000 people will begin filing into the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) for a very un-Australian sporting spectacle - American football.

The LA Rams take on the San Francisco 49ers in their opening National Football League (NFL) fixture, the first time the country has hosted a meaningful, non-exhibition regular season game.

The match sold out months ago, with more than half the crowd expected to be people living outside the state of Victoria. On the official ticket resale site, a restricted view seat is priced at more than A$650 (£350/US$470).

"Walking down the street, it's AFL finals week and you wouldn't even know," says Thomas McMillan, host of the NFL podcast Any Given Sunday Australia.

"It's all NFL everywhere. There are bars that are nothing but 49ers bars or Rams bars. We have a Ram Tram getting around the district. When you're in Melbourne and AFL isn't visible, it shows how big this is at the moment."

Kickoff at 10.35am local time on Friday may not be typical for local fans, but meets the demands of prime time US television schedules and their advertisers.

The league held its first international match in 2007, and over the past two decades the overseas matches have become a long-term strategy to attract supporters and their dollars.

Nine games outside the US are scheduled for the upcoming season, including three in London. But Melbourne is the furthest that players and US-based fans will have to travel.

"Obviously there are question marks when you hear you are playing in Australia," 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey told a press conference this week.

"But it has been so cool… the food's incredible, the coffee's great."

That caffeine reference was perhaps as much to the time zone, as nod to the city's famous café culture.

Melbourne is a mind-warping 17 hours ahead of California where both teams are based, and much of the pre-match attention has been on the two teams and their contrasting approaches to trying to "beat" the jet lag.

For the 49ers, who arrived late last week, their players have had time to get over the long journey, adjust to the time zone, acclimatise and practice at a nearby stadium.

Controversially, the LA Rams are taking things to the other extreme, planning to arrive on Thursday morning local time on a charted Qantas A380 superjumbo, play on Friday, and get back to the US west coast shortly afterwards, in theory to prepare for their next match with minimum disruption to the player's body clocks.

"Definitely it's a gamble," says McMillan. "If they don't quite get things right after the 16-hour flight, you still might have that jet lag, even though you're trying to avoid it."

"And not everyone can sleep on planes," says his co-host Danny Webb. "Whether you're in first class, business class, whatever it is, you're still on a plane."

"And", adds McMillan: "And they're six foot six most of them, so it's going to be even tighter seats".

Despite it technically being a "home" game for the Rams, who bid for NFL marketing rights in Australia under the leagues Global Markets programme, this all means it is the San Francisco 49ers that have more of a presence around Melbourne this week.

And while most practice sessions have been behind closed doors, there have been player appearances at a rally for fans and an AFL match, while ex-stars turned up at that most Australian of traditions, the weekly fundraising "sausage sizzle" at the country's most high-profile hardware chain.

American sports journalist Dontay Atkinson predicts this fan engagement will be reflected inside the stadium and that the MCG will be "heavily red" (the 49ers colour), accusing the Rams of doing "exactly jack squat to sell the NFL brand or connect with Australians".

Writing on X he added: "Fly in, fly out, no contact. I'm sure the Aussies feel great about that snub."

McMillan says he can understand the approach by the Rams, who are seen as contenders for the 2027 Superbowl.

"They're looking at this as a game they need to win," he says.

"We do feel a bit snubbed, and feel the 49ers are doing the right thing,

"But it is their job, so that's where the Rams coaching staff has gone 'nah, we're taking this approach'.

"I just worry that they have missed the boat of ingraining themselves as the Australian team. It leaves it open for others, and the 49ers have really jumped on that."

The LA Rams insist there has been no snub, though speaking to the BBC, the club's Head of International Stephanie Cheng dodged the question of whether she would have preferred her players to have been in town this week.

"It's really a culmination of more than four years of work," she said. "It's not just about game week. We have long term rights."

Cheng says the Rams are the only NFL team with a membership programme for Australian fans, and that it has sent coaches into schools and communities to promote "flag football" – the non-contact version of the sport which will feature in the LA 2028 Olympics.

She also points to regular earlier visits by star players including running back Kyren Williams in March. This week its cheerleaders have visited US military bases in Australia before coming to Melbourne, and the franchise has installed a 22-yard floating football field on Melbourne's Yarra River serving as a fan zone.

"From day one, when we've come to Australia, there's been incredible enthusiasm," Cheng said.

While no Australian players will be on the field on Friday, there are dozens playing US college football and a handful in the NFL.

Most are punters, kicking specialists tapped up after showing their prowess playing AFL or rugby league.

But it is the success of Jordan Mailata, an offensive left tackle with the Philadelphia Eagles, who in 2025 became the first Australian to play in, and win, a Superbowl that was a "major turning point in Australia's fandom of the NFL " says Webb.

"Seeing an Australian in what we'd called a skilled position and then winning a Superbowl. It doesn't get better than that".

Friday's game is the first of three matches in Melbourne to be held over four years, under a contract between the NFL and the state of Victoria.

The league's preference, says Gerrit Meier, managing director and head of NFL International, is to have annual games in Australia similar, to the way the game has grown in the UK.

"We're working off the hypothesis that we need to make a commitment to a market," he told Reuters.

And while many US-based supporters are not fans of the international fixtures, these games are here to stay, says Webb, and the hype and the sell-out crowd in Australia augurs well for it to become a long-term fixture,

"I had mates four years ago asking why are you doing an NFL podcast? It's not a big sport here," he said.

"And now every single one of those mates are asking me for tickets for the game."

items.title: Watch: How a community living under demolition orders from Israel view UK sanctions
items.summary: Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson visits the Palestinian community of Khan al Ahmar, and the neighbouring Israeli settlement of Maale Admumim.
items.content:
UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank have triggered a series of Israeli counter-measures against UK nationals and organisations.

The sanctions came after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of settlement homes in the strategically important so-called E1 area east of Jerusalem, plans that have drawn widespread international condemnation.

The development would in effect divide the West Bank in two, and isolate East Jerusalem.

The BBC's Middle East Correspondent Lucy Williamson has been to the Palestinian community of Khan al Ahmar in the E1 area, and also to the neighbouring Israeli settlement of Maale Admumim.

items.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
items.summary: Declassified documents show Spanish and Moroccan authorities were alerted to social media calls for a mass migrant crossing the day before tens of thousands entered Ceuta.
items.content:
Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.

The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.

On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.

Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.

At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants .

In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".

The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades."

It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.

The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.

Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.

However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.

Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".

But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.

"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.

Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".

The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.

Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have foreseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".

A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".

Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.

"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."
